questions.question: What does the Model Context Protocol standardize?
options: How a model host and an external system exchange capabilities and tool calls
The weights, architecture, and training data that define the model itself
The one programming language in which every compliant server must be written
The retail pricing and per-token billing terms of every hosted model API
questions.explanation: MCP is a protocol for the messages between a host and a server, not the model, a price list, or a language mandate.

questions.question: In MCP, what is a client responsible for?
options: It trains the underlying model that decides which server tool to call
It holds exactly one connection to one server on behalf of the host
It stores a full copy of every connected server's data on local disk
It meters usage and bills the end user for each tool call that runs
questions.explanation: A client lives inside the host and maintains exactly one connection to one server; the host embeds one or more clients.

questions.question: Why does MCP reduce an N times M integration problem to N plus M?
options: It removes the need for authentication or authorization between host and server
It forces every server to run inside one single shared operating-system process
Each host speaks MCP once and each server exposes it once, so any pair connects
It permanently caches every response so an integration never runs a second time
questions.explanation: One shared protocol means a host is written once and a server is written once, and they interoperate without custom glue per pair.

questions.question: How does a client learn which tools a server offers?
options: It reads a config file the user must write by hand for each server tool
It guesses the tool names directly from the server's operating-system process name
It recompiles the host together with the server's full source code at startup
It requests the tool list at runtime and the server returns each tool's schema
questions.explanation: Discovery is part of the protocol: the server advertises its tools as data, so a client can use tools it was not built with.

questions.question: A client sends a tools/call request naming a tool the server does not expose. What should a conformant server do?
options: Return a JSON-RPC error whose code and message are keyed to the request id
Silently pick and run the closest matching tool it does happen to expose
Return an empty result object as though the requested call had succeeded
Immediately terminate the transport connection without sending any response
questions.explanation: An unknown tool is a client error the server reports as a structured JSON-RPC error, not a crash, a silent substitution, or a fake success.

questions.question: When a tool result crosses back from the server into the host, why does it matter for security?
options: The model is unable to read tool results at all, so they remain completely inert
It is untrusted content entering the model's context across a trust boundary
The host process owns the server, so any content it returns is inherently trusted
The result is always encrypted in transit, so its contents can be safely ignored
questions.explanation: The server is a separate program; its output is untrusted input to the model, which is why the trust boundary sits at the tool result.
